title: Ensuring Maintainable Architecture
overview: Maintainability is the ease with which software can be corrected, enhanced, adapted or have its performance improved, and it usually dominates lifecycle cost. The deck splits it into changeability (modifiability) and analyzability, then covers how architecture style, code-level tactics, defer-binding techniques, logging and monitoring, and automated safeguards such as fitness functions make change cheap and safe. For the exam, expect to pick tactics for a change scenario and compare how monolith, microservices and event-driven styles support change.
big_ideas: The lecture cites maintenance costs of **80–90% of lifecycle cost** to motivate designing for change; treat this as a cited estimate rather than a universal percentage.
The lecture focuses on **modifiability and analyzability**, supported by reliable-change practices; the earlier ISO 25010:2011 model also names modularity, reusability and testability.
Four modifiability tactics: **split modules, increase cohesion, reduce coupling, defer binding**.
Cost of change vs cost of development trade off: code change (high/low), configuration (medium/medium), customizable by implementers (medium/high), customizable by end user (low/high).

Events let a new consumer use an existing event without changing its producer, provided the event has the needed information. Versioned schemas support evolution but still require compatibility discipline.
Code-level tactics: contain change, extensible interfaces, design techniques that ease change, variation points, standard extension points.
Analyzability needs automated error detection, good logging (agent, storage, dashboard, correlation id) and monitoring (JMX/SNMP).
Reliable change: version control, automated tests, CI, rollback, infrastructure as code, hypothesis-driven testing and **fitness functions** guarding architecture rules.

sections.title: What maintainability is and why it matters
sections.summary: The IEEE definition, the lifecycle-cost argument and the practical benefits of maintainable software.

notes.lead: The **ease** with which a system or component can be **modified** to:
items: **Correct faults**
**Improve performance or other attributes**
**Adapt to a changed environment**
Lecture cites an **80–90% maintenance share**
→ motivation for **reducing future change effort**
**Architectural decision**: **where likely changes justify investment**
notes.foot: Don't assume that percentage applies to **every project**.

notes.h: What maintainable software lets you do
items: **Fix a bug** without **introducing a new one**
**Add features** without **altering existing ones**
**Improve usability and performance**
Make a **fix that prevents future bugs**
**Support new environments**, **operating systems** or **tools**
**Onboard new developers**

terms.def: Ease of correcting faults, improving attributes or adapting to a changed environment.

check.q: Two designs for a loyalty system: A ships in 2 months with the reward rules hard-coded; B takes 3 months with the rules isolated behind an interface and held in configuration. Marketing expects to change the rules monthly for 5 years. Which do you choose?

items: **About 60 rule changes** expected → the extra month is repaid by **cheaper, safer changes**
**Most lifecycle cost falls in maintenance** (the lecture cites **80-90%**)
**A** would need a **code change, test and release** for every rule tweak
a.foot: If the system were a **short-lived campaign**, A would be the better choice.

check.q: A team says it will 'make the code maintainable later, once we have users'. Do you agree?

items: **Detailed refactoring can wait**
**Boundaries, interfaces and variation points** are **architectural** → cost far more to add once code depends on their absence
Put them **where change is likely** now, and defer the rest
a.foot: How much to invest depends on the **expected changes** and the **system's lifetime**.

sections.title: Sources of change and how to incorporate it
sections.summary: Change is ubiquitous; the choice is who can make it and what it costs to build and to apply.

sub: cost depends on **how modifiable the architecture is**
mostly **B2B**: each **tenant** has a **dedicated implementation team**

notes.h: Rule: invest where change is likely
items: The **more you invest up front** in making **change possible without code**
→ the **cheaper each later change**
→ so **invest where change is likely**
**Modifiability** and **analyzability**
Then **practices for reliable change**
**Reliable change** is a **supporting practice**, not a replacement name for the **ISO model’s maintainability sub-characteristics**

terms.def: Ease of changing the system; also called changeability.
Deferred, gap, vague or open-ended requirements signal that change is coming.

check.q: For an insurance product, actuaries change pricing factors monthly, and the screen layout changes about once a year. Which way of incorporating change suits each?

items: **Pricing factors** → **configuration**, or **end-user customisation** by the actuaries: the change is **frequent** and each code change would be expensive
**Layout** → a **code change** is fine: it is **rare**, and the development cost of making it customisable would not pay back
a.foot: Invest in **cheap change where change is likely**.

check.q: A requirements document says 'the system shall support other payment methods in future' and 'reporting: to be decided in phase 2'. What does this tell the architect?

a.lead: **Open-ended and deferred requirements** signal a **high likelihood of change** → put **variation points** there:
items: A **payment-method interface**
**Reporting** fed from **well-defined data**
a.foot: Spending the same effort on areas with **stable requirements** would be wasted.

check.q: A B2B SaaS product has five enterprise clients, each with a dedicated implementation team, and each wants its own approval rules. Which change mechanism fits?

items: Build **configurable rules or workflows** that each client's team sets up
**Development cost is high**, but each change is **medium-cost** and needs **no core code change**
**Full end-user customisation** would cost even more to build → isn't needed when **trained implementers** do the changes

visuals.title: Ways to incorporate change
rows: Any kind of change is possible
Depends on how modifiable the architecture is
Built into original implementation; mostly B2B, dedicated team per tenant
Difficult, but best value when done correctly

sections.title: Architecture styles and modifiability
sections.summary: The four tactics, and how monolith, microservices and event-driven styles apply split, cohesion and coupling.

items: **Split modules**
**Increase cohesion**
**Reduce coupling**
**Defer binding**
notes.foot: The **first three** are examined at **architecture level** and **code level**.

items: **Unstructured** → **tangled classes** behind **one UI**
**Layered monolith** → **presentation**, **business rules**, **persistence**, **database**: separates concerns by **technical layer**
**Modular monolith** → groups classes into **modules and components**, all still **deployed as one unit (a quantum)**
notes.foot: **Changes stay inside a layer or module only if boundaries are respected.**

items: Put **capability-specific logic and data** behind **service APIs**
Allow **independent deployment** when **contracts remain compatible**
**Splitting services does not automatically enforce low coupling**
Add an **analytics consumer** of an **existing event** **without changing producers**, if its **payload already meets the need**
**Broker topology** → **routes events** among **processors**
**Mediator topology** → **coordinates workflow steps**
**Events still couple** consumers to **payload meaning** and **delivery behaviour**
Stores **versioned payload schemas**
**Messages identify the schema used** (lecture illustrates an **id** and **version**)
**Consumers use that definition** to **read the payload**
Makes **schema evolution manageable**
**Incompatible field or meaning changes** still require **coordination** and **compatibility checks**

terms.def: How closely a module's responsibilities belong together; increase it.
Store of versioned message schemas used by producers and consumers.
Event-driven component that orchestrates a workflow across processes.

check.q: A team wants to add a fraud-analytics consumer to the existing OrderPlaced events, but the event does not carry the customer's IP address, which the model needs. Is this still a change-free extension?

items: A **new consumer** avoids **producer changes** only when the **existing payload** already meets its needs
Here the **producer must add the field**, ideally as an **optional addition** registered as a **compatible new schema version** → existing consumers keep working
a.foot: Events still **couple consumers** to the payload's **content and meaning**.

check.q: Five microservices read and write one shared customer table, and renaming a column needs a coordinated release of all five. What has gone wrong?

a.lead: **Shared data has coupled the services**, defeating **independent deployment**.
items: **Fix**: give the customer data a **single owning service**, and have the others use its **API or events**
**Alternative**: if that split is not worth it, a **modular monolith** may contain changes just as well at **lower operational cost**

check.q: A producer renames the field 'amount' to 'total' and registers the change as version 2 in the schema registry. Are consumers safe?

items: The **registry** stores **versioned schemas** and lets consumers find the one a message uses
But an **incompatible change** still breaks consumers that expect 'amount'

check.q: In a layered monolith, adding a 'gift card' feature touches the presentation, business and persistence layers. Would a modular monolith help?

items: A **modular monolith** groups code by **business module**
→ a **gift-card module** contains its own UI, logic and data access, and the change stays inside it
a.foot: It still **deploys as one unit**, so you don't get **independent deployment**; that would need **services**.

visuals.title: Architecture styles and change
rows: Change contained by layers, modules and components
Independent services, each with own data, behind API layer
Independent changes when data and API boundaries hold
Add consumers when existing event content is sufficient

sections.title: Code-level maintainability tactics
sections.summary: Five design tactic groups contain changes and provide extension points; reliable-change practices are covered later.

items: **Encapsulation** → keep change **inside a component** (e.g. a **Discount Engine** using the **Strategy pattern**)
**Separation of concerns** → **clear distinct responsibilities**
**Single point of definition** → **data types**, **algorithms**, **config**, **schemas** defined **once**, so **no need to synchronise changes**
**Object parameters** can grow **without a method-signature change**
**Optional fields** and **flexible JSON/XML formats** can support **compatibility**
**Keep old fields and meanings usable**
**Test existing consumers**
**Version incompatible changes** with a clear **support policy**
notes.foot: **A flexible format alone does not make a change safe.**

items: **Abstraction and layering** → **minimal impact** of one part on others
**Generalisation** → group **similar scenarios** into a **general pattern** handled by **one component**
**Inversion of control** → components can be **reconfigured**
Make elements **replaceable**
**Parameterise changeable properties** in **configuration**
**Separate physical from logical processing** → convert **many physical formats** into **one logical structure**
**Break processes into steps** → change is **confined to some steps**
**ODBC/JDBC** → for **different databases**
**JSON/SOAP/REST** → for **calling services**
**JCA** → the **standard Java adapter**

terms.def: Hiding details inside a component so callers are unaffected by change.
Define each type, algorithm or config once.
Components are wired or configured externally, allowing reconfiguration.
Deliberate place where behaviour can be swapped or configured.

check.q: A public API method has 7 parameters, and clients keep breaking whenever a parameter is added. What would you change?

items: **Pass a single request object** → new **optional fields** can be added without changing the **method signature**

items.t: **Old clients must still be served correctly**

items: **Version the API** for changes that cannot be compatible

check.q: A bank receives statements from 12 partners in CSV, XML and fixed-width formats, and parsing logic is spread across the system. What would you change?

items: **Convert at the edge**: each physical format → one **standard logical structure**
Use **only that structure** in the rest of the system
→ a **new partner format** then changes only a **converter**
a.foot: The cost is one more **mapping layer** to maintain.

check.q: A discount rate of 0.15 is hard-coded in 9 places, and the last change missed one. Which tactic would have prevented this?

items: **Define the rate once**, in configuration or a constant used everywhere → a change never has to be **synchronised across copies**
**Parameterising it in configuration** also lets you change it **without a code release**

check.q: A JSON API adds a mandatory field to every request. Is it backward compatible because the method signature is unchanged?
check.a: No. Existing callers omit the new field and may fail validation. Add it as optional with suitable behaviour for old callers, or version the breaking contract and migrate consumers.

visuals.title: Contain changes at a format boundary

steps.label: Physical formats
steps.detail: Different systems may send the same business information in different structures. A new format should not force changes throughout the application.

steps.label: Adapters
steps.detail: Convert each external representation into one agreed internal logical structure. Add or change the relevant adapter when a physical format changes.

steps.label: Logical processing
steps.detail: The rest of the system uses the logical structure. A format-only change stays at the edge; a genuine change in business meaning still affects the model.

sections.title: Defer binding: customisation and workflow engines
sections.summary: Push decisions to run time so users or implementers change behaviour without recompiling.

items: Making the application **customisable at run time**
**Fully user-customisable** needs **good UX expertise** and **domain understanding**
Deck's example: **Amplitude analytics** → **customisable cohort analyser** lets users analyse **retention across cohorts** **without writing data-munging logic**
An **admin or implementer designs a workflow** for a **specific tenant or role**
The **workflow logic is persisted**
At **run time** the engine **deserialises** the tenant or role's workflow
...and **executes it**, **calling domain logic**
notes.foot: Result: **logic customisation without recompiling**, e.g. a **different approval workflow per client**.

items: Many engines provide a **visual designer**
→ **lowers the skill** needed to **change behaviour**
= the '**customizable by implementation team**' end of the **change-cost table**

terms.def: Postpone choosing behaviour until run time, by configuration or user customisation.
Component that executes persisted, designable workflows at run time.

check.q: Each of 30 corporate clients wants a different expense-approval chain, and the chains change a few times a year. How would you design it?

items: An **implementer designs** each client's workflow
It is **stored per tenant**
**At run time** the engine loads and executes it, calling **shared domain logic**
→ changes need **no recompiling or redeployment**
a.foot: The cost is **building or adopting the engine**, and limiting workflows to the steps it supports.

check.q: For a 3-month MVP, a team proposes fully end-user-customisable reports. Do you agree?

items: **End-user customisation** has the **lowest change cost** when done well, but the **highest development cost**
It needs **strong UX** and **domain understanding** that an MVP rarely has
**Instead**: ship a few **fixed reports** → learn which variations users actually want → add customisation where that demand is clear

steps.label: Admin designs workflow
steps.detail: An admin or implementer designs a workflow for a specific tenant or role, often with a visual designer.

steps.label: Workflow persisted
steps.detail: The workflow logic is saved in workflow persistence, not compiled into the application.

steps.label: User calls API
steps.detail: A user from a tenant or role calls the API controller, which passes the request to the workflow engine.

steps.label: Engine executes
steps.detail: The engine loads that tenant's workflow from persistence and executes it, invoking domain logic 1, 2...

sections.title: Analyzability: detecting and diagnosing problems
sections.summary: How to detect problems, find the root cause and monitor systems, including logging in microservices.

items: How do we **detect problems**?
**Identify the root cause**?
**Make and deploy the fix**? (the last step is **like any other change**)
**Automated error detection and reporting** → e.g. **UNIX core dump**, **log file monitoring**
**Good logging practice** → **enough information to support an investigation**
**Logging agent**
**Log storage**
**Log dashboard** with **search**
**Fluentd** → the **agent**, collecting logs from the **nodes**
**Elasticsearch** → the **storage**
**Kibana** → the **dashboard**
So **entries from one request** can be **matched across services**
**Central storage alone** does **not show which records belong together**
**Missing identifiers** → reconstruction **harder and less reliable**

terms.def: Standard protocols for monitoring and managing applications (Java) and network devices.
Identifier passed across services to trace one request in the logs.

check.q: A checkout error appears in the logs of four services, but nothing links the entries. What would you add?

items: **Created at the entry point** and passed with **every call and event**
**Written in each service's log entries**
→ the entries for one request can be pulled together for **root-cause analysis**
a.foot: **Central log storage alone** does not show which records belong together.

check.q: Container logs disappear when pods restart, and engineers SSH into nodes to grep for errors. What would you change?

a.lead: **Add the three logging components** (**EFK** is the lecture's example stack):
items: An **agent** on each node that ships logs
**Central log storage**
A **dashboard with search**
→ logs **survive restarts** and can be **searched across services**
a.foot: The cost is running and **sizing the logging infrastructure** itself.

check.q: A legacy application crashes every night and leaves nothing useful behind. Which analyzability tactics apply?

items: **Automated error detection and reporting**: **core dumps**, **log file monitoring** that raises **alerts**
**Logging** with enough **context** to investigate
**Monitoring through standard protocols** such as **JMX** or **SNMP**
a.foot: Together these turn 'it crashed' into a **diagnosable fault**.

steps.label: Fluentd
steps.detail: Collects logs from the different nodes in the Kubernetes cluster.

steps.label: Elasticsearch
steps.detail: Stores and indexes the collected logs for searching.

steps.label: Kibana
steps.detail: Presents and searches the logs; use a correlation id to trace one request across microservices.

sections.title: Reliable change and fitness functions
sections.summary: Practices that make changes safe, and fitness functions that automatically guard architectural rules.

items: **Track changes** in **version control**
**Automate tests** and **build/integration checks**
Support **deployment rollback**
Manage **environment configuration as code**
Apply **hypothesis-driven testing**
Integrate **secrets management** **without committing secret values**
notes.foot: **Automating release/deployment** extends the **delivery process** beyond **CI alone**.

notes.lead: An **automated check** that an **architectural characteristic still holds**. Deck's pipeline:
items: **Unit test**
**Build** and **deploy**
**Integration** and **end-to-end tests**
**Promote**
A **unit test** using a **dependency-analysis tool (JDepend)**
Asserts that **persistence** and **web** packages **depend on util** as allowed
→ the **build fails** if any code **breaks layer dependencies** in a **layered architecture**

terms.def: Automated test of an architectural characteristic, run in the delivery pipeline.
Versioned definitions of infrastructure and environment configuration, integrated with separate secrets management.

check.q: The architecture rule says the web layer must not call the persistence layer directly. Code reviews keep missing violations. What would you add?

items: An **automated test** using a **dependency-analysis tool** → **fails the build** when web code depends on persistence packages
It checks the rule on **every build**, which **review cannot do reliably**
a.foot: It guards **only the rules you actually encode**, so add checks for other key characteristics as well.

check.q: A release breaks checkout, and reverting takes 3 hours because the database migrations cannot be undone. What should the release process have included?

items: **Reversible or backward-compatible migrations**
The ability to **redeploy the previous version quickly**
**Why**: even tested changes fail in production → **fast reversal limits the damage**
a.foot: **Version control**, **automated tests** and **environment configuration as code** make that reversal reliable.

check.q: A release works in staging but fails in production, because the two environments were configured by hand and differ. A developer suggests committing the production passwords into the repository so everything is in one place. Respond.

items: **Manage environment configuration as code** → staging and production are built from the **same versioned definitions**
**Do not commit secret values** → integrate a **secrets-management tool**, and **reference secrets** from the configuration
a.foot: **Reproducible environments** without **leaked credentials** make change reliable.

steps.label: Build and deploy
steps.detail: Automated build and deployment to a test environment.

steps.label: Integration and end-to-end
steps.detail: Verify components and complete flows together.

steps.label: Fitness checks
steps.detail: Code quality, resiliency, observability, performance, compliance, security code analysis and operability standards are checked automatically; passing leads to promote.

sections.title: Code quality tools
sections.summary: Static analysis tools help track relative quality, but only if you understand the metrics.

items: **FindBugs**, **Checkstyle**, **PMD**, **SonarQube** → **code issues and metrics**
**CodeCity** → **visualising code structure**
notes.foot: **Learn what a result reveals** rather than memorising product names as **proof of quality**.

items: **Understand what each metric means**
Useful for the **relative quality progression** of **one code base over time**
**Not for absolute comparison between systems**
This topic stresses **analyzability**, **changeability**, **stability** and **testability**

items.t: For an **ISO 25010:2011 classification** question, use (from the **foundations lecture**):

terms.def: Platform that analyses code quality and reports issues and metrics.

check.q: A quality dashboard improves after a release. Does that prove the architecture is easier to maintain?

items: **Check what changed** in the metrics, and whether they reflect **relevant change** or **diagnostic effort**
**Combine trends** with actual **change scenarios** and **fitness checks**
a.foot: A score is evidence for its **measured properties**, not all maintainability.

check.q: A manager wants to rank three teams' systems by their static-analysis scores to decide bonuses. Do you agree?

items: These metrics are useful for **tracking one code base's relative progress over time**, not for **comparing different systems** in absolute terms
**Size, language and domain differ** between systems
Using them for **bonuses** also **invites gaming**
a.foot: Compare each team against its **own trend**, alongside **real change effort**.

exam_angles.q: A product's discount and eligibility rules change every quarter, and three of its 20 enterprise clients need their own approval flow. The business wants changes shipped without redeployment. Recommend a design and its costs.

a.lead: **Defer binding** for the kinds of change that recur.
items: **Rule parameters in configuration**, which business users edit through an **admin screen**, behind a **single point of definition**
A **workflow engine** runs **per-tenant approval flows** designed by the **implementation team**
**Encapsulate the domain actions** the workflows call, and define the **supported variation points**
**Costs**: this lowers the cost of each change but **raises development cost**, and needs **UX and domain work**
a.foot: Behaviour **outside the variation points** still needs a **code change**, so choose the variation points from the **expected changes**.

exam_angles.q: An online learning platform has a layered monolith, five teams and frequent collisions between releases. It plans to add analytics, recommendations and partner integrations over two years. Compare a modular monolith, microservices and an event-driven approach for modifiability, and recommend one.

a.lead: **Recommend modularising first**, then extracting services where **team collisions** are worst, and publishing events for the new consumers.

sub: **Business modules contain changes** and avoid **distributed costs**
But everything still **deploys as one unit** → **release collisions remain**
**Independent deployment** per capability, if each **owns its data** and APIs **evolve compatibly**
But they add **operational cost**, and **shared tables** or **call chains** can still spread change
Analytics and recommendations can **subscribe to existing events** (CourseCompleted, LessonViewed) without **producer changes**
Only if the **payloads carry what they need**, with a **schema registry** and **compatibility rules**

exam_angles.q: A public REST API has about 200 external consumers you do not control. Over the next year you must add fields, rename one concept and change one response structure. Which code-level tactics keep the API evolvable?

items: **Request and response objects** with **optional fields** → additions don't break signatures
**Renamed concept**: add it alongside the old one, and **deprecate** the old name with a **support period**
**Structural change**: put it in a **new API version**, keeping the old one running during migration
**Encapsulate the implementation** behind the API, define the **shared data types once**, and use **standard formats**
**Test existing consumer contracts**
a.foot: Flexible **JSON syntax** alone does not guarantee **compatibility**.

exam_angles.q: During an incident, a payment fails somewhere across six microservices. It takes four hours to find the cause because logs are local to each container and have no common identifier. Redesign for analyzability.

items: **Automated error detection and alerting** → the failure is noticed rather than reported by users
**Centralise logs** with an agent, storage and searchable dashboard (for example **EFK**) → they survive container restarts
**Propagate a correlation id** from the entry point through every call and event → one request's entries can be retrieved together
**Log enough context**, such as inputs, the dependency called and the error
**Expose metrics** through **standard monitoring**
a.foot: The fix itself is then deployed like any other change, through the **reliable-change pipeline**.

exam_angles.q: A layered system's dependency rules are eroding, releases often break production, and rollbacks are manual. Design a pipeline that makes change reliable and stops further erosion.

items: **Keep everything in version control**, including **environment configuration as code**, with secrets in a **secrets manager**
**Automated tests** on each change: unit, integration and end-to-end

sub: A **dependency test** that fails on **layer violations**
Plus **performance, security, resiliency and observability** checks

items: **Automate deployment** with a **tested rollback path** and **reversible migrations**
**Hypothesis-driven testing** for risky changes
a.foot: Fitness functions **guard only what they encode**, so add rules as the architecture evolves.
